title: A Key Finds a Name, Not Relatives

scenes.visual: Title card 'A Key Finds a Name, Not Relatives' fades in over a sandy Chesapeake Bay shoreline with a blue crab at the water's edge. Same WORLD and COLOUR MAP as the first film (NAVY domain, INDIGO kingdom, PURPLE phylum, TEAL class, GREEN order, GOLD family, ORANGE genus, CORAL RED species). The KEY is drawn as a path of white fork signposts on a slate-grey trail; each fork has one trait on each arm. Seven animal cards: BROOK TROUT, BLUE CRAB, EASTERN OYSTER (grey two-part shell), SEA STAR (orange, five arms), EARTHWORM (pink, ring-like segments), SPONGE (yellow, full of holes, fixed to a rock), SEA NETTLE (pale jellyfish with trailing tentacles). Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: How could a few two-choice questions give you the name of a crab? You find it on the shore of the Chesapeake Bay, and you do not know what it is. A key can tell you.
scenes.visual: A cartoon hand points at the blue crab on wet sand. A blank name tag hangs above the crab with a question mark. Text on screen: 'What is its name?'
scenes.narration: How could a few two-choice questions give you the name of a crab? You find it on the shore of the Chesapeake Bay, and you do not know what it is. A key can tell you.

scenes.tts: The first film put living things in nested boxes, to show how they are grouped. This film uses a different tool, called a dichotomous key. Both tools matter, but they do different jobs.
scenes.visual: A small thumbnail of the first film's nested boxes, navy to coral, slides to the top-left corner and stays there. Beside it the word 'dichotomous key' writes itself, with 'two choices at every step' in small grey letters underneath.
scenes.narration: The first film put living things in nested boxes, to show how they are grouped. This film uses a different tool, called a dichotomous key. Both tools matter, but they do different jobs.

scenes.tts: A dichotomous key is a series of two-choice steps about traits you can see. Each step splits the path in two. You follow the choice that fits, until you reach a name.
scenes.visual: A slate-grey trail runs left to right. At the first white signpost it forks into two arms. A small walking figure stops at the fork, looks at both arms, and picks one. Labels: 'step = two choices', 'traits you can see'. The trail ends at a name tag.
scenes.narration: A dichotomous key is a series of two-choice steps about traits you can see. Each step splits the path in two. You follow the choice that fits, until you reach a name.

scenes.tts: Our key holds seven animals, each from a different phylum. Step one asks, fins or no fins? The crab has no fins, so we go on. Step two asks, jointed legs or no jointed legs? The crab has jointed legs.
scenes.visual: The seven animal cards fan out at the start of the trail. Fork 1 signpost: 'fins' (arm to the BROOK TROUT card) / 'no fins: go to 2'. The crab card walks down 'no fins'. Fork 2 signpost: 'jointed legs' / 'no jointed legs: go to 3'. The crab's jointed legs flash, and it walks down 'jointed legs'. A step counter reads 'steps: 2'.
scenes.narration: Our key holds seven animals, each from a different phylum. Step one asks, fins or no fins? The crab has no fins, so we go on. Step two asks, jointed legs or no jointed legs? The crab has jointed legs.

scenes.tts: The path ends at a name, Kally-neck-teez sap-ih-dus, the blue crab. Look at the whole key. The trout comes off the path first, the crab second, and the oyster third.
scenes.caption: The path ends at a name, Callinectes sapidus, the blue crab. Look at the whole key. The trout comes off the path first, the crab second, and the oyster third.
scenes.visual: The name tag over the crab fills in: 'Callinectes sapidus' in italics. Camera pulls back to show the whole key as a vertical ladder of six forks: trout, crab, oyster, sea star, earthworm, then sponge and sea nettle at the last fork. The crab card glows; the trout card above and the oyster card below get thin outlines labelled 'neighbors'.
scenes.narration: The path ends at a name, Callinectes sapidus, the blue crab. Look at the whole key. The trout comes off the path first, the crab second, and the oyster third.

scenes.tts: Now keep every question, but change their order. Ask about the two-part shell and the five arms before the jointed legs. Watch the branches redraw.
scenes.visual: The fork signposts lift off the trail, shuffle in the air like cards, and land in a new order: 1 fins, 2 shell of two hinged halves, 3 five arms around a center, 4 jointed legs, 5 ring-like segments, 6 fixed and full of holes / swims with a bell. The trail redraws itself to match. Label in the corner: 'same questions, new order'.
scenes.narration: Now keep every question, but change their order. Ask about the two-part shell and the five arms before the jointed legs. Watch the branches redraw.

scenes.tts: Run the crab again. It takes more steps now. But the path ends at the same name, Kally-neck-teez sap-ih-dus. Every animal keeps its name. Only its neighbors change.
scenes.caption: Run the crab again. It takes more steps now. But the path ends at the same name, Callinectes sapidus. Every animal keeps its name. Only its neighbors change.
scenes.visual: The crab card walks the new trail: no fins, no two-part shell, no five arms, jointed legs. Step counter reads 'steps: 4' beside a faded 'before: 2'. The name tag fills in with the same 'Callinectes sapidus'. In the ladder view the crab now sits between the SEA STAR above and the EARTHWORM below, both outlined and labelled 'new neighbors'.
scenes.narration: Run the crab again. It takes more steps now. But the path ends at the same name, Callinectes sapidus. Every animal keeps its name. Only its neighbors change.

scenes.tts: The crab now sits right next to the sea star. Has the crab become more closely related to the sea star?
scenes.visual: Close-up of the crab card and the sea star card side by side in the new key. Text on screen: 'Closer relatives now?'
scenes.narration: The crab now sits right next to the sea star. Has the crab become more closely related to the sea star?

scenes.visual: Hold the crab and sea star side by side. Card in the centre: 'Pause and predict: yes or no?' A thin countdown bar shrinks over 5 seconds.

scenes.tts: No. Drop the animals into the boxes from the first film. The crab is in phylum Arth-ro-poda. The sea star and the oyster are each in a different phylum. The crab shares only two boxes with each of them, the domain and the kingdom.
scenes.caption: No. Drop the animals into the boxes from the first film. The crab is in phylum Arthropoda. The sea star and the oyster are each in a different phylum. The crab shares only two boxes with each of them, the domain and the kingdom.
scenes.visual: The first film's nested boxes return, same colours. The crab drops in and stops inside its own PURPLE box labelled 'phylum Arthropoda'. The sea star drops into a separate purple box labelled 'echinoderms', and the oyster into another labelled 'mollusks'. All three sit inside the same INDIGO 'kingdom Animalia' box inside the NAVY 'domain Eukarya' box. Tally strips under the sea star and the oyster each light 2 squares, navy and indigo, labelled '2 of 8 boxes shared with the crab'.
scenes.narration: No. Drop the animals into the boxes from the first film. The crab is in phylum Arthropoda. The sea star and the oyster are each in a different phylum. The crab shares only two boxes with each of them, the domain and the kingdom.

scenes.tts: The crab shares just two boxes with the trout, too. In either order, the boxes stay the same. Moving a question cannot make two animals closer relatives.
scenes.visual: The trout drops in and lands in a separate purple box labelled 'phylum Chordata', inside the same indigo and navy boxes. Its tally strip lights 2 squares: '2 of 8 boxes shared with the crab'. Above the boxes, the two key ladders (old order and new order) sit side by side; arrows from each point to the same unchanged nested boxes.
scenes.narration: The crab shares just two boxes with the trout, too. In either order, the boxes stay the same. Moving a question cannot make two animals closer relatives.

scenes.tts: Why does this happen? This key asks about traits that are easy to see, not who is related. So its order alone does not show who is related. The boxes show how one classification groups them. To draw the boxes, scientists compare body parts, what living things do, and DNA.
scenes.visual: Left: the key ladder with each fork's trait word glowing: 'fins', 'shell', 'five arms', 'jointed legs'. A label: 'chosen because easy to see'. Right: the nested boxes, labelled 'shows how one classification groups them'. A rule card slides up between them: 'Key: finds the name. Boxes: show the grouping.'
scenes.narration: Why does this happen? This key asks about traits that are easy to see, not who is related. So its order alone does not show who is related. The boxes show how one classification groups them. To draw the boxes, scientists compare body parts, what living things do, and DNA.

scenes.visual: End card: the hexagon mascot Hex holds a small fork signpost in one hand and a nested-box sign (navy to coral) in the other. Line on screen: 'A key finds the name; shared boxes show the grouping.'
